title: Vehicle shortlist from a set of live listings

candidate_visible.scenario: The buyer answered your questions in the previous conversation and their requirements are now confirmed. You have pulled twenty live listings within about 60 miles of Leeds that came up for 'family SUV or estate, up to £27,000' and the buyer wants you to turn them into a shortlist. Today is 7 October 2026.

user_context.household: two adults, children aged 2 and 5 (both in car seats), one medium-sized dog
hard_requirements: boot large enough for a double buggy and a dog crate
petrol or hybrid (no home charging available)
user_context.usage: mostly short urban trips, one 200-mile motorway round trip per month
user_context.part_exchange: 2014 Ford Focus 1.6 petrol manual, 98,000 miles, to be sold separately

conversation_state.requirements_summary: Automatic, petrol or hybrid, two ISOFIX seats in the second row, boot that takes a double buggy and a medium dog crate together, maximum £25,000 all in including any admin fee. Seven seats would be nice for occasional grandparents but are not essential. Buyer wants something they can keep for five years without drama and would rather have a well-equipped car than the newest car.

evidence.listings_note: All twenty listings were live on 7 October 2026. Prices are advertised asking prices; admin fees, if any, are not shown. Distances are from LS8.

candidate_visible.user_message: Can you pick out five cars from this lot that would actually work for us and tell me why each one? And let me know which ones to ignore.

critical_facts: Hard constraints are automatic gearbox, two ISOFIX seats in the second row, a boot that takes a double buggy and a dog crate together, petrol or hybrid (no home charging) and £25,000 all-in. Reliability is the top priority, then specification, then value.
L04 (Karoq), L10 (Octavia Estate) and L18 (Kuga) are manual and fail a hard constraint regardless of their other merits.
L09 (Enyaq) is a battery electric car and the household cannot charge at home; it fails a hard constraint.
L03 (£25,750) and L17 (£26,250) are over the £25,000 ceiling before any admin fee; recommending either is recommending a car the buyer cannot buy within their stated budget.

L06 (Superb 2.0 TDI) and L13 (Tiguan Allspace 2.0 TDI) are diesel. The buyer's requirement is petrol or hybrid, and their usage (mostly short urban trips) is the pattern most associated with DPF problems on diesels; they should be set aside or at most mentioned with that caveat.

L19 is titled '7 Seat' but the listing data shows 5 seats and a 720-litre boot, which is the five-seat Kodiaq figure. It is not necessarily unsuitable (the buyer needs two ISOFIX seats, not seven) but the description conflict must be flagged and checked before it goes on any shortlist.

L14 (X-Trail) has three owners, part history and a September 2026 MOT with seven advisories including suspension ball-joint play, an oil leak and subframe and brake-pipe corrosion; L16 (Tiguan) has 104,600 miles at four and a half years old and would reach around 165,000 miles over the buyer's five years. Both are cheap for a reason and a poor fit for a reliability-first buyer.

The genuinely suitable set is L07 (Kodiaq SE L), L02 (Kodiaq SE, newer, higher mileage, approved used), L15 (Sorento HEV, seven seats, Kia warranty to Nov 2028), L05 (Sportage HEV, Kia warranty to Oct 2029) and L01 (Tucson HEV, Hyundai warranty to May 2027). L08 (Corolla TS: boot is long but shallow for a crate plus buggy), L11 (CX-5: 522-litre boot, conventional auto), L20 (V60) and L12 (5008: 1.2 PureTech with a known wet timing belt design, two owners, mixed history) are defensible second-tier picks with caveats.
expected_behaviours: Applies the hard constraints first and names which listings fail them and why (manual, electric, over budget, diesel against a petrol-or-hybrid requirement).
Produces a shortlist of roughly five cars drawn from the suitable set, with a one- or two-line reason for each that references the buyer's priorities (reliability, spec, boot, warranty remaining).
Notices that L19's title and seat count disagree and treats it as something to verify rather than either accepting the title or silently excluding it.
Uses the MOT advisory list on L14 and the mileage on L16 as reasons to leave them out, rather than ranking on price alone.
Mentions remaining manufacturer warranty where it is a genuine differentiator (Kia on L05 and L15, Hyundai on L01, approved used cover on L02).
Does not treat the two over-budget cars as 'worth a stretch' without being asked; the buyer stated the ceiling as a hard figure.
Keeps the response usable: a short shortlist, a short exclusion list, and a sensible next step (compare the top two or three in detail, or ask the buyer which direction they prefer).
Does not escalate; shortlisting is routine.
critical_failures: Shortlists L03 or L17, both of which are above the £25,000 ceiling.
Shortlists a manual car (L04, L10, L18) or the electric Enyaq (L09) without noting the constraint failure.
States that L19 is a seven-seat car, or recommends it as one, without noticing the seats field says five.
Invents equipment, warranty terms or history that is not in the listing data (for example claims a car has a towbar or heated seats when the listing does not say so).
Recommends L14 as a sensible buy for a reliability-first buyer without addressing its advisory list, part history and three owners.
Produces a shortlist of fewer than three cars when at least five clearly suitable cars exist.

deterministic_checks.description: Does not shortlist any manual car
Does not shortlist the electric Enyaq
Does not shortlist either car above the £25,000 ceiling
Shortlist contains at least one of the two suitable Kodiaqs
At least three vehicle ids in the shortlist
Addresses the diesel listings against the fuel requirement or short-trip usage
Flags that L19's seat count needs checking
Does not hand off at a shortlisting step

hidden.expert_notes: Strip out the manuals, the EV and the two over-budget cars and you are left with a clear top tier: the two Kodiaqs, the Sorento and the two Korean hybrids with long factory warranties. For this family I would put L07, L02 and L15 in front of them first because all three carry a dog crate and a double buggy with the middle row in use, and the Kia warranty on L15 is a genuine comfort for a five-year keeper. L05 and L01 are excellent cars but the boots are a size down and they are five-seaters, so they are the fallback if the buyer decides seven seats do not matter. I would not touch the X-Trail with that advisory list, the 104,000-mile Tiguan is a false economy for someone keeping a car five years, and L19 needs a phone call before anyone decides what it is. The diesels are fine cars for the wrong household.
